region.text: Kyoto and Yamashiro Province, where the Ōnin War began

ledger.note: 1467: the Ōnin War breaks out in Kyoto and 'initiated the Sengoku period'. The page puts the most intense fighting 'in Kyoto and Yamashiro Province'; the state begins as that war zone and takes the rest of Japan from the shogunate in 1468.

region.text: Kyoto and Yamashiro Province, most intense fighting of the war

ledger.note: 1467: Kyoto becomes a battlefield. 'The fighting started in March when a Hosokawa mansion was burned', between the Eastern Army of Hosokawa Katsumoto and the Western Army of Yamana Sōzen; the Ashikaga dossier dates the start to May 1467 from the same page.

region.text: everything outside the Kyoto remnant: the provinces of the shugo and the daimyo

ledger.note: 1468: outside Kyoto the shogunate no longer rules. 'After the Ōnin War, the Ashikaga bakufu completely fell apart' and 'the war had spread to the rest of Japan'; the year is Cliopatria's (Warring States Japan begins in 1468, the Ashikaga shape shrinks to the Kyoto remnant), not the page's. Re-read 2026-10-18: the Onin War page still gives no year for the bakufu losing control outside Kyoto ('the war had spread to the rest of Japan', undated; 'Disintegration of the power of the shogunate' is undated in the infobox), so 1468 stays Cliopatria's.

region.text: Kyoto and Yamashiro Province, where the war was fought

ledger.note: 1477: the Ōnin War ends in Kyoto. Ōuchi Masahiro 'left the area on 17 December 1477'; 'By 1477, ten years after the fighting had begun, Kyoto was nothing more than a place for mobs to loot.'

region.text: the entire province of Kaga, 'the south and western portion of Ishikawa Prefecture'

ledger.note: 1488: the Kaga Ikkō-ikki takes Kaga Province. Sengoku timeline: the Kaga Rebellion establishes the Kaga ikki, which 'assumed control of the entire province of Kaga'; the page says it remained independent for nearly 100 years. The Ikkō-ikki page dates the same rebellion to 1486 ('overthrew the governor of Kaga Province and established self-rule'); 1488 is used. The region is the south and west of modern Ishikawa Prefecture (Kaga Province page), approximated by a 50 km circle at Kanazawa within Ishikawa.

region.text: the cells Cliopatria adds on the southern Oshima Peninsula around Hakodate

ledger.note: 1552: the shape extends into southern Hokkaido (Oshima Peninsula, Hakodate side). Page silent on this year: the Matsumae clan page dates only the 1590 march fief; Cliopatria's 1552 shape adds nine cells there. Wajin (Japanese) settlements on the peninsula are the land concerned; a gap-filler should find a dated page for the Kakizaki/Matsumae holding. Re-read 2026-10-18 (History of Hokkaido page): it says only that in the Muromachi period (1336-1573) 'the Japanese established a settlement at the south of the Oshima Peninsula' and dates Takeda Nobuhiro's killing of the Ainu leader Koshamain to 1457; no 1552 date, so the confidence stays 1.

region.text: the Kyoto remnant to which the shogunate had shrunk

ledger.note: 1573: Nobunaga ends the Ashikaga shogunate and takes Kyoto. 'Ashikaga shogunate abolished: September 2, 1573'; the Sengoku page records that Nobunaga expelled Ashikaga Yoshiaki from Kyoto in 1573, ending the shogunate. Cliopatria adds the Kyoto cells one year early, in 1572.

1573: the Sengoku period gives way to the Azuchi-Momoyama period under Nobunaga. The page dates the period 1568 to 1603 (its navbox 1573 to 1603), 'Nobunaga overthrew Yoshiaki and dissolved the Ashikaga Shogunate in 1573' and the infobox says 'Ashikaga shogunate abolished: September 2, 1573'. The infobox line 'Oda Nobunaga captures Kyoto: October 18, 1573' is not used: it falls after the page's own abolition date and the page dates the period from 1568. Same state and colour; Cliopatria's Seshat ids jp_sengoku_jidai and jp_azuchi_momoyama share the row.

1573: the shogun's residence is Azuchi. Infobox: 'Azuchi (Shogun's residence) (1573-1582)'; Heian-kyo stays the Emperor's residence and de jure capital. The first seat this dossier records after the Kyoto war zone of 1467: the pages name no seat for 1468-1572 (identity/capitals).

region.text: the entire province of Kaga, retaken from the Ikkō-ikki

ledger.note: 1580: the Kaga ikki ends. Shibata Katsuie page: 'In 1580, he led an army, which included his general Sakuma Morimasa in a fight against the Kaga Ikko-ikki at Kanazawa Gobo' (the year of the Kaga campaign is the page's; that this ended the ikki's rule is the researcher's reading). The Kaga Province page says only that 'The area was eventually conquered by Oda Nobunaga's general Shibata Katsuie', with no year, and the Sengoku page gives no end year ('nearly 100 years'); the Sengoku and Azuchi-Momoyama pages give 1580 for the Ishiyama Hongan-ji surrender after the 11-year siege.

1582: the centre returns to Kyoto. Nobunaga dies on 21 June 1582 ('Death of Oda Nobunaga: June 21, 1582'); the infobox lists Heian-kyo for 1582-1600, and Hideyoshi rules from Osaka Castle (built 1586).

region.text: Busan, where the divisions landed, Hanseong (10 June 1592) and Pyongyang (20 July 1592)

ledger.note: 1592: Hideyoshi's army lands in Korea. Infobox '23 May 1592 - 16 December 1598'; the Japanese 'arrived at Hanseong first, on 10 June' and 'entered the deserted city of Pyongyang' on 20 July 1592 (Azuchi-Momoyama page: 'occupied Seoul by May 1592', a different date for the same event). Hatched around the three cities the page names; the land between is the researcher's reading.

1593: the Japanese leave the north. 'The Japanese were forced to withdraw as far as the southern part of the Korean peninsula by January 1593' (Azuchi-Momoyama page); the Imjin War page has Katō Kiyomasa 'forced to abandon Hamgyong Province due to cold and supply problems'.

region.text: the southern part of the Korean peninsula ('as far as the southern part of the Korean peninsula by January 1593')

ledger.note: 1593: the Japanese hold the south. Azuchi-Momoyama page: 'The Japanese were forced to withdraw as far as the southern part of the Korean peninsula by January 1593' (the source of the date). The Imjin War page's sentence that the invading forces 'withdrew to the peninsula's southern coastal regions' and could not be dislodged describes the aftermath of the 1597 second invasion, not 1593; it supports the same zone for 1597-1598, and the Battle of Jiksan page has the Japanese, after 16 October 1597, 'retreated to their fortified bastions along the coasts'. The Ulsan page shows them holding Ulsan's Tosan fortress in January-February 1598. The pages name no castle list; the hatched zone is the south coast of Gyeongsang.

region.text: the southern coastal regions held since 1593

ledger.note: 1598: the Japanese leave Korea. Hideyoshi died (18 September 1598, Azuchi-Momoyama page), the Japanese were 'defeated at the Battle of Noryang' and 'ordered to withdraw to Japan by the new governing Council of Five Elders'; infobox end 16 December 1598, result 'Status quo ante bellum'.

region.text: the Eastern Army's lands, the Tokugawa camp

ledger.note: 1600: the eastern half goes to the Tokugawa. Sekigahara page: 'Eastern army victory' on 21 October 1600 under Tokugawa Ieyasu against the Western Army of Ishida Mitsunari; 'Tokugawa clan gains nominal control of all Japan'. The page has no map of the two camps (only a table of daimyo and koku), so the two camps' lands are Cliopatria's split: the Warring States Japan shape falls from 325,141 km2 (1595, without Korea) to 165,165 km2 (1600) and the Tokugawa Shogunate 1600 shape (163,913 km2) is the other half. Mirrors tokugawa-shogunate ledger/0 (found, 10/1600). The region is the Tokugawa 1600 shape intersected with this state's 1595 shape, so the Ryukyu cells in the Tokugawa row, which this state never held, are not counted.

region.text: the western half of Japan, the Western Army's side

ledger.note: 1600: Sekigahara hands the western half to the Tokugawa. 'Eastern army victory' on 21 October 1600; 'Tokugawa clan gains nominal control of all Japan'; 'roughly 87 daimyo had their domains confiscated' and Ieyasu 'redistributed domains worth 6.8 million koku'. The western half is Cliopatria's 1600 shape for this row; the Toyotomi keep Osaka under Hideyori until the Tokugawa act on it.

region.text: all that remained of the Western Army's half, now under 'nominal control of all Japan'

ledger.note: 1600: the Sengoku-Azuchi-Momoyama state ends at Sekigahara. 'Occurred on October 21, 1600'; 'generally considered to be the beginning point of the Tokugawa shogunate'; Ieyasu is appointed shogun by Emperor Go-Yōzei in 1603. The land passes to the Tokugawa shogunate.

wars.name: Ōnin War
wars.outcome: No victor: it ended in December 1477 with the Ashikaga bakufu reduced to a Kyoto power and the provinces in the hands of daimyo; 'The war initiated the Sengoku period'.
wars.note: The two camps were the Eastern Army of Hosokawa Katsumoto and the Western Army of Yamana Sōzen; the page puts the war 'throughout Japan, though most intense fighting in Kyoto and Yamashiro Province'.

wars.name: Kaga Rebellion
wars.outcome: The Kaga ikki assumed control of the entire province and kept it for nearly 100 years.
wars.note: The Ikkō-ikki page puts the rebellion in 1486.

wars.name: Ishiyama Hongan-ji War
wars.outcome: Oda took Ishiyama Hongan-ji 'in 1580 after an 11-year siege' (Ikkō-ikki page); the Kaga Province page says Shibata Katsuie conquered Kaga without a year.
wars.note: The Sengoku page's timeline dates the start to 1570 ('Battle of Anegawa and the beginning of the Ishiyama Hongan-ji War'); the Ikkō-ikki page's '11-year siege' ending 1580 would count back to 1569. Start corrected from 1569 to 1570 by the jk-01-c reviewer, 2026-10-18.

wars.name: Shikoku campaign (Hideyoshi)
wars.outcome: 'The daimyo of the Shikoku Chōsokabe clan surrendered to Hideyoshi in July, 1585.' Internal to the state; the outline does not change.
wars.note: The Sengoku page's timeline puts Chōsokabe Motochika's rule of all Shikoku in 1583.

wars.name: Kyushu campaign (Hideyoshi)
wars.outcome: 'Hideyoshi conquered Kyushu in the Kyushu Campaign (1586-1587) from the Shimazu clan.' Internal to the state; the outline does not change.

wars.name: Siege of Odawara

wars.name: Japanese invasions of Korea (Imjin War)

zones.text: the southern coastal regions of Korea held by the Japanese 1593-1598
the 1597 advance: Jiksan, near Cheonan, 'the furthest point the Japanese ever got to reaching Hanseong during the Second Invasion' (16 October 1597)

wars.outcome: Joseon and Ming victory; territorial change 'Status quo ante bellum'; the Japanese left in December 1598 after Hideyoshi's death and the defeat at Noryang.
wars.note: 'Japan invaded Korea again in 1597, and gained initial successes on land' and was then 'halted and withdrew to the peninsula's southern coastal regions' (Imjin War page, re-read 2026-10-18). The Battle of Jiksan page dates the furthest Japanese advance, near modern Cheonan, to 16 October 1597, followed by 'an orderly retreat south'; neither page says the Japanese held Jeolla or Chungcheong, so the 1597 advance is a zone of the war, not an occupation event. The 1593 date of the southern zone rests on the Azuchi-Momoyama page ('by January 1593'); the Imjin page does not describe 1593.

wars.name: Siege of Ulsan
wars.outcome: 'Withdrawal of Korean and Ming forces': an 'unsuccessful Ming-Joseon attempt to capture Ulsan from the Japanese', 26 January to 19 February 1598.

wars.name: Battle of Sekigahara
wars.outcome: Eastern Army (Tokugawa) victory on 21 October 1600; 'Tokugawa clan gains nominal control of all Japan'.
wars.note: The page gives Sekigahara, in Mino Province (Gifu Prefecture), as the field; the two camps' lands are Cliopatria's 1600 split.

certainty.note: A land of competing daimyo: no treaty or survey line is on the pages, and the one shape per year is Cliopatria's abstraction. The sea coasts are exact; the Hokkaido foothold (1552) and the Korean occupation (1592-1598, hatched) are the softest edges; Kaga (1488-1580) was held by the Ikkō-ikki.

notes:
Written by Phase B agent jk-01-c on 2026-10-18 from nine pages (the budget): Sengoku period, Azuchi-Momoyama period, Matsumae clan, Imjin War, Battle of Sekigahara, Ōnin War, Ikkō-ikki, Siege of Ulsan, Kaga Province.

What this row is: Cliopatria's 'Warring States Japan' (1468-1601) draws the whole archipelago as one shape for the time when the Ashikaga shogunate held only the Kyoto remnant (the Ashikaga row's 1468-1571 shapes). The real actors, the daimyo domains, the Ikkō-ikki provinces and Oda and Toyotomi's growing hegemony, are not states on the map; the Sengoku domains are for jk-01-x. This dossier keeps the single shape, starts it with the Ōnin War (1467, one year before Cliopatria) and ends it at Sekigahara (21 October 1600, Cliopatria 1601), and records only the border moves the pages date: Kaga (1488-1580), the Hokkaido foothold, the Kyoto remnant (1573), the Korean occupation (1592-1598) and the split at Sekigahara. Hideyoshi's unifications (Shikoku 1585, Kyushu 1587, Odawara 1590) are wars with empty zones: they are inside the shape.

Corrections to Cliopatria: (1) the 1572 shape adds Kyoto a year early (shogunate ended 1573); (2) the 1595-1599 shape draws South Korea as Japanese land: wrong, replaced by hatched occupation events; (3) the 1600 shape is the Western Army's half and ends at the battle; the 1601 year is the Tokugawa's. The 1552 Hokkaido cells have no dating page (confidence 1).

Not settled: (a) the dates of the Korean campaign after July 1592 come from the Azuchi-Momoyama and Ulsan pages because the Imjin War text returned by the fetcher stopped in July 1592; the second invasion of 1597 names no land, so it is a war entry only. (b) Kaga starts in 1488 (Sengoku) or 1486 (Ikkō-ikki page), and its end in 1580 is inferred (Kaga Province page undated). (c) The Yamashiro ikki (1485) and the Iga ikki (independent from 1477, destroyed 1581 per the Sengoku table) held land too but are not recorded: no end date for the first and no pages beyond the table for the second; jk-01-x or a gap-filler may add them. (d) The Matsumae/Kakizaki holding in southern Hokkaido and the Ainu counterpart need a dossier or a page. (e) The infobox areas: none on the Sengoku or Azuchi-Momoyama pages, so Cliopatria's 320,000-325,000 km2 (Japan without Hokkaido and Ryukyu) could not be compared.

Counterparts: ashikaga-shogunate (dossier exists, jk-01-b; its ledger records the matching 1467 contest, 1468 loss, 1477 contest end and 1573 dissolve against this slug), joseon (jk-02), kaga-ikko-ikki (written in this batch), tokugawa-shogunate (this batch), ming-dynasty. Region names used that the gazetteer may lack: none beyond Natural Earth names; the Kaga region is a Kanazawa 50 km circle inside Ishikawa because 'Kaga Province' is not a gazetteer entry.
